answer.rationale: Three signals converge on the release as the proximate cause: (1) p99 write-path latency began climbing roughly 30 minutes after the deploy, consistent with a regression rather than organic load growth; (2) the degradation is confined to the primary region, which argues against a broad infrastructure or capacity issue and against a partner-side outage; (3) settlement traffic is at daily peak, so the regression is amplified now and will continue to compound if left in place. memory_b1 (day 18) is the closest structural analog — a release-correlated error spike resolved cleanly by rollback with no customer impact. memory_b2 (regional failover) is a tempting alternative, but failover shifts load to a secondary region during peak settlement writes, introducing replication lag and split-write risk at the worst possible moment; it also does not remove the bad code, so the secondary region inherits the regression. Adding capacity treats a symptom, not the cause. Circuit breakers and read-replica routing address read-path or dependency failures, neither of which matches the write-path-primary-only signature. Rolling back restores the last known-good build, stops the latency climb at its source, and does so within the single-intervention window. If the rollback does not restore p99 within the expected window, regional failover becomes the next-window escalation.
